Three towns with lives of their own

Editable 240 × 240 map variants. Central roads and the river are six tiles wide, with their standard boundary connections. Side streets, yards and upper rooms offer routes around the buildings.

Rough layouts using existing assets. Two peaceful residents in each town have short authored lines. These maps are not automatically assigned to a campaign.

Linden Square

A meeting hall became a clinic; the ration office stayed upstairs.

The market still feeds the town. Beds have replaced the meeting-hall benches, while ration records and a private office occupy the upper floor next door.

Open town in the editor
  1. Meeting hall / clinic — A public hall hastily divided into a ward and a treatment room.
  2. Ration office / private flat — Crates and the public counter below; a comfortable private room and telephone upstairs.
  3. Cooperative shop — A full stockroom behind an almost empty shop counter.
  4. Garden house — A small home with the dining table still laid and a little garden behind it.
  5. Market store — Pallets and open crates link the store to the outdoor stalls.
  6. Workers boarding house — A shared dining room below and simple beds upstairs.
  7. Square canteen — Tables face the square; supplies are pushed into the back corner.
  8. Garden tool shed — Tools, spare parts and an improvised workbench.

Last Shift

A working town whose machines outlasted its last payday.

Finished parts wait on pallets, the canteen is set for a shift that never arrived, and the manager has kept the only comfortable upstairs room.

Open town in the editor
  1. Repair shop — An unfinished lathe job, boxed finished parts, and a clean service aisle.
  2. Manager office / flat — The payroll counter is downstairs; the manager kept a private room above it.
  3. Tool lockup — The useful tools have been packed away; loose spares remain on the bench.
  4. Worker family home — A modest family table and a chest packed for departure.
  5. Shift lodgings — A common room and four beds whose owners never came back for their things.
  6. Shift canteen — The tables are set; fuel and the cooking area are outside in the yard.
  7. Dispatch store — Finished goods arranged beside the loading apron, with nobody left to collect them.

Floodmark

A bridge, a customs house and homes turned into an evacuation station.

Cargo was hauled off the low quay into a dry warehouse. The customs house still has its records, but the family house is now a small first-aid post and the waiting hall holds stranded travellers.

Open town in the editor
  1. Waiting hall / shelter — Waiting benches, luggage crates and a room now used as an overnight shelter.
  2. North-bank family home — A family dining room looking down toward the bridge.
  3. Quay tool shed — Rope and repair supplies are represented by a bench, toolbox and packed chest.
  4. Dry warehouse — Cargo rescued from the low quay is stacked on the dry side of the road.
  5. Customs house / lookout — Records and inspection tables below; a bridge-facing office above.
  6. House / first-aid post — A family home converted to a two-bed first-aid post.
  7. Vacated quay house — The household has packed; only a bare table and an open chest remain.
  8. Bridge kitchen — A shared kitchen provides a reason for people on both banks to keep the bridge open.
  9. Shelter store — Dry bedding and relief supplies, represented by stacked crates and chests.

Use Sector presets to reopen these, then Save to make another named variant in the same configuration folder. Coordinates and building notes are preserved in each map's sectorTemplate.town metadata.
